concepts.title: Computation Graph
concepts.one_liner: A computation graph represents a neural network as a series of modular blocks or layers chained together.
concepts.content:
A key idea of neural nets is to decompose computation into a series of layers. Layers are treated as modular blocks that can be chained together into a computation graph. For example, a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) can be visualized as a sequence of these modular layers.

(see figure: In this chapter we will visualize neural nets as a sequence of layers, which we call a computation graph.)
concepts.motivation_md: Decomposing complex functions into a graph of simpler operations makes it easier to implement automatic differentiation and organize the architecture of deep learning models.
concepts.recap_md: - Decomposes complex computations into modular, chained blocks.

slots.motivation: Decomposing complex functions into a graph of simpler operations makes it easier to implement automatic differentiation and organize the architecture of deep learning models.

concepts.title: Forward Pass for a Layer
concepts.one_liner: The forward pass is the operation where a layer transforms inputs into outputs.
concepts.content:
Each layer takes in some inputs and transforms them into some outputs; this is called the $\texttt{forward}$ pass through the layer. If the layer has parameters $\theta$, they are considered an input to a parameter-free transformation:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}&= f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}},\theta) \end{aligned}$$

(see figure: Forward operation of a neural net layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: The forward pass is the fundamental mechanism by which a neural network processes input data to generate a prediction or representation.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps input $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and parameters $\theta$ to an output $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$.

slots.motivation: The forward pass is the fundamental mechanism by which a neural network processes input data to generate a prediction or representation.
slots.key_passage: - Maps input $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and parameters $\theta$ to an output $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$.

(see figure: Forward operation of a neural net layer.)

concepts.title: Backward Operation
concepts.one_liner: The backward operation is a layer-specific function used in computation graphs to calculate gradients.
concepts.content: The backward operation is a special operation defined for each layer in a computation graph. Just like the forward pass, it is modular and relies on the structure of the graph to propagate information.
concepts.motivation_md: To train a network, we need to know how the loss changes with respect to every parameter; the backward operation provides a modular way to compute these gradients using the chain rule.
concepts.recap_md: - A modular operation defined for each layer to facilitate gradient calculation.

slots.motivation: To train a network, we need to know how the loss changes with respect to every parameter; the backward operation provides a modular way to compute these gradients using the chain rule.
slots.key_passage: - A modular operation defined for each layer to facilitate gradient calculation.

concepts.title: Backpropagation: Reuse of Computation

position.section_title: The Trick of Backpropagation: Reuse of Computation

concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation efficiently computes gradients by reusing shared terms from the chain rule across different layers.
concepts.content:
Consider a computation graph that is a chain of functions $f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots f_2 \circ f_1$, where each function $f_l$ is parameterized by $\theta_l$. To optimize these parameters with respect to a scalar loss $J$, we compute gradients like $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_1}$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_2}$ using the chain rule. 

(see figure: Basic sequential computation graph.)

(see figure: Computation graph as a tree.)

When writing out these gradients, many terms are shared:

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_1} &= \left( \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_L} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_3}{\partial \mathbf{x}_2} \right) \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_2}{\partial \mathbf{x}_1} \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_1}{\partial \theta_1} \\ \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_2} &= \left( \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_L} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_3}{\partial \mathbf{x}_2} \right) \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_2}{\partial \theta_2} \end{aligned}$$

The trick of backpropagation is to evaluate the shared product (highlighted in parentheses) only once and reuse it for all subsequent gradient calculations, rather than computing each layer's gradients independently.
concepts.motivation_md: Calculating gradients independently for every parameter in a deep network would be computationally prohibitive. Reusing intermediate results reduces the complexity from exponential to linear with respect to the number of layers.
concepts.recap_md: - Identifies shared terms in the chain rule expansion of gradients.

slots.motivation: Calculating gradients independently for every parameter in a deep network would be computationally prohibitive. Reusing intermediate results reduces the complexity from exponential to linear with respect to the number of layers.
slots.key_passage: - Identifies shared terms in the chain rule expansion of gradients.

The trick of backpropagation is to evaluate the shared product (highlighted in parentheses) only once and reuse it for all subsequent gradient calculations, rather than computing each layer's gradients independently.

concepts.title: Backpropagation as Dynamic Programming
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation is an application of dynamic programming, as it stores and reuses intermediate results to solve a complex problem.
concepts.content: The strategy of calculating shared terms once and reusing them in subsequent calculations is known as dynamic programming. Backpropagation applies this general algorithmic strategy to the computation of gradients in a neural network.
concepts.motivation_md: By framing backpropagation as dynamic programming, we can understand it as an efficient way to solve the sub-problems of gradient calculation by caching intermediate results.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses dynamic programming to avoid redundant calculations.

slots.motivation: By framing backpropagation as dynamic programming, we can understand it as an efficient way to solve the sub-problems of gradient calculation by caching intermediate results.
slots.key_passage: - Uses dynamic programming to avoid redundant calculations.
slots.example: The strategy of calculating shared terms once and reusing them in subsequent calculations is known as dynamic programming. Backpropagation applies this general algorithmic strategy to the computation of gradients in a neural network.

concepts.title: Local Gradient Arrays (g and L)
concepts.one_liner: The local gradient arrays $\mathbf{g}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ represent partial derivatives of the cost and the layer output, respectively, at a single operating point.
concepts.content:
(see figure: A generic layer in the computation graph. The braces represent the part of the computation graph we need to consider in order to evaluate $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$, $\mathbf{L}$, and $\mathbf{g}in$.)

Two key shorthand arrays are used to track partial derivatives for backpropagation:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_l&\triangleq \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_l} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{grad of cost with respect to } \mathbf{x}_l \quad [1 \times |\mathbf{x}_l|]\\
    \mathbf{L}&\triangleq \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \theta]} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{grad of layer}\\
    &\quad\quad \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} \triangleq \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{\quad with respect to layer input data} \quad [|\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}| \times |\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}|]\\
    &\quad\quad \mathbf{L}^{\theta} \triangleq \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial \theta} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{\quad with respect to layer params} \quad [|\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}| \times |\theta|]
\end{aligned}$$

All these arrays represent the gradient at a single operating point, defined by the current values of the data and parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: To perform backpropagation efficiently, we need a standardized way to represent the sensitivity of the cost function and the layer outputs to their inputs and parameters. These arrays provide the necessary building blocks for applying the chain rule across layers.
concepts.recap_md: - $\mathbf{g}_l$ is the gradient of the cost $J$ with respect to the layer activations $\mathbf{x}_l$.

slots.motivation: To perform backpropagation efficiently, we need a standardized way to represent the sensitivity of the cost function and the layer outputs to their inputs and parameters. These arrays provide the necessary building blocks for applying the chain rule across layers.
slots.key_passage: - $\mathbf{g}_l$ is the gradient of the cost $J$ with respect to the layer activations $\mathbf{x}_l$.

\end{aligned}$$

All these arrays represent the gradient at a single operating point, defined by the current values of the data and parameters.

concepts.title: Parameter Update Rule
concepts.one_liner: The parameter update rule uses the product of the output gradient and the layer's parameter gradient to adjust weights and minimize cost.
concepts.motivation_md: The ultimate goal of training a neural network is to find parameters that minimize the cost function. This rule provides the specific mechanism for adjusting those parameters based on the calculated gradients.
concepts.recap_md: - The gradient with respect to parameters is the product of the output gradient $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ and the local parameter gradient $\mathbf{L}^{\theta}$.

slots.motivation: The ultimate goal of training a neural network is to find parameters that minimize the cost function. This rule provides the specific mechanism for adjusting those parameters based on the calculated gradients.
slots.key_passage: - The gradient with respect to parameters is the product of the output gradient $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ and the local parameter gradient $\mathbf{L}^{\theta}$.

concepts.title: Backpropagation Recurrence Relation
concepts.one_liner: The backpropagation recurrence relation allows for the iterative computation of error signals by sending gradients backward through the network.
concepts.content:
Computing the gradient of the cost with respect to inputs, $\mathbf{g}$, requires evaluating the chain rule across all layers between $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$ and $J$. This can be computed iteratively: once $\mathbf{g}_l$ is known, $\mathbf{g}_{l-1}$ is found via a single matrix multiplication. This is summarized by the recurrence relation:

$$\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{backpropagation of errors}
\end{aligned}$$

This recurrence is the essence of backpropagation: it sends error signals (gradients) backward through the network, starting at the last layer and iteratively applying the relation to compute $\mathbf{g}$ for each previous layer. In deep learning libraries like PyTorch, this value is typically stored in a `.grad` field associated with each variable.
concepts.motivation_md: Calculating gradients for deep networks would be computationally prohibitive without an efficient method. This recurrence relation breaks the complex global gradient calculation into simple local matrix multiplications.
concepts.recap_md: - Error signals $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ are computed by multiplying the subsequent gradient $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ by the local Jacobian $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}$.

slots.motivation: Calculating gradients for deep networks would be computationally prohibitive without an efficient method. This recurrence relation breaks the complex global gradient calculation into simple local matrix multiplications.
slots.key_passage: - Error signals $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ are computed by multiplying the subsequent gradient $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ by the local Jacobian $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}$.

concepts.title: Backward Function for a Generic Layer
concepts.one_liner: The backward function for a generic layer takes the input data, parameters, and output gradient to produce the input gradient and parameter gradient.
concepts.content: The `backward` function for a generic layer consists of an operation that takes three inputs ($\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \theta, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$) and produces two outputs ($\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta}$). ![`backward` for a generic layer. We use the color to indicate parameter gradients.](figures/backpropagation/mod_block_backward.png) In this process, the color red is used for data/activation gradients being passed backward through the network, while yellow indicates parameter gradients.

concepts.title: Forward Pass through the Network

position.section_title: The Full Algorithm: Forward, Then Backward

concepts.one_liner: The forward pass evaluates the network layer by layer, starting from the input data to produce a sequence of activations.
concepts.content:
To prepare for gradient updates, we first compute a forward pass through the entire network. This involves starting with input data $\mathbf{x}_0$ and evaluating each layer sequentially to produce the sequence $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$.

(see figure: Forward pass.)

During this pass, data and activations are passed forward through the network, often represented visually with green indicators.
concepts.motivation_md: Gradients depend on the specific values of activations at each layer. The forward pass is necessary to establish these "operating points" before the backward pass can calculate derivatives.
concepts.recap_md: - The forward pass computes activations $\mathbf{x}_l$ sequentially from $l=0$ to $L$.

slots.motivation: Gradients depend on the specific values of activations at each layer. The forward pass is necessary to establish these "operating points" before the backward pass can calculate derivatives.
slots.key_passage: - The forward pass computes activations $\mathbf{x}_l$ sequentially from $l=0$ to $L$.

(see figure: Forward pass.)

During this pass, data and activations are passed forward through the network, often represented visually with green indicators.

concepts.title: Backward Pass through the Network

position.section_title: The Full Algorithm: Forward, Then Backward

concepts.one_liner: The backward pass iteratively evaluates gradients from the last layer to the first to obtain parameter gradients for the entire network.
concepts.content:
Following the forward pass, we compute a backward pass by iteratively evaluating the gradients $\mathbf{g}$ and obtaining the sequence $\mathbf{g}_L, \mathbf{g}_{L-1}, \ldots$, as well as the parameter gradients for each layer.

(see figure: A schematic diagram of the backpropagation process in a neural network. Red arrows flow from right to left, starting with a value of 1 entering a loss derivative block $\mathcal{L}'$, then passing...)
concepts.motivation_md: The backward pass is the core algorithm for training; it efficiently propagates the error from the output back to every weight in the network, allowing for simultaneous optimization of all parameters.
concepts.recap_md: - The backward pass computes the sequence of gradients $\mathbf{g}_l$ in reverse order.

slots.motivation: The backward pass is the core algorithm for training; it efficiently propagates the error from the output back to every weight in the network, allowing for simultaneous optimization of all parameters.
slots.key_passage: - The backward pass computes the sequence of gradients $\mathbf{g}_l$ in reverse order.

concepts.title: Backpropagation Over Data Batches
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation in batch mode computes the average gradient over a set of datapoints to update parameters for the entire batch.
concepts.motivation_md: Training on single examples can be noisy and inefficient. Batch mode allows for more stable gradient estimates and takes advantage of parallel computing hardware like GPUs.
concepts.recap_md: - The batch gradient is the average of the gradients calculated for each individual datapoint.

slots.motivation: Training on single examples can be noisy and inefficient. Batch mode allows for more stable gradient estimates and takes advantage of parallel computing hardware like GPUs.
slots.key_passage: - The batch gradient is the average of the gradients calculated for each individual datapoint.

concepts.title: Linearity of Gradients
concepts.one_liner: The gradient of a sum of terms is equal to the sum of the gradients of each individual term.
concepts.motivation_md: This property is fundamental to machine learning because it justifies why we can compute gradients on individual examples or small batches and combine them to optimize a global objective function.
concepts.recap_md: - The gradient of a sum is the sum of the gradients.

slots.motivation: This property is fundamental to machine learning because it justifies why we can compute gradients on individual examples or small batches and combine them to optimize a global objective function.
slots.key_passage: - The gradient of a sum is the sum of the gradients.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a Linear Layer
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation for a linear layer involves computing gradients with respect to inputs, weights, and biases using matrix multiplications and outer products.
concepts.content:
A linear layer is defined in the forward direction as $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$, where $\mathbf{W}$ is an $[M \times N]$ matrix and $\mathbf{b}$ is an $M$-dimensional vector. To perform backpropagation, we require the gradients of this function with respect to its inputs and parameters. The individual scalar gradients are:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}[i,j] &= \frac{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[i]}{\partial x_{\texttt{in}}[j]} = \mathbf{W}[i,j] \\ \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{W}}[i,jk] &= \frac{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[i]}{\partial \mathbf{W}[j,k]} = \begin{cases} x_{\texttt{in}}[k], &\text{if} \quad i == j\\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\ \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{b}}[i,j] &= \frac{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[i]}{\partial \mathbf{b}[j]} = \begin{cases} 1, &\text{if} \quad i == j\\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$

These imply that $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{I}$. The `backward` implementation for a linear layer uses these to compute:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{W}\\ \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{b}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} \end{aligned}$$

(see figure: The forward and backward matrix multiples for a linear layer.)

The gradient with respect to the weights, $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}}$, simplifies to an outer product between the input vector and the output gradient:

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}} = \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$$

(see figure: Matrix multiply for parameter gradient of a linear layer.)

(see figure: Linear layer forward and backward.)

These operations are easily implemented using matrix multiplication primitives as shown in the following pseudocode:

```python
class linear():
    def __init__(self, W, b, lr):
        self.W = W
        self.b = b
        self.lr = lr
        
    def forward(self, x_in):
        self.x_in = x_in
        return matmul(W,x)+b
    
    def backward(self,J_out):
        J_in = matmul(J_out,W)
        dJdW = matmul(self.x_in,J_out)
        dJdb = J_out
        return J_in, dJdW, dJdb
    
    def update(self, dJdW, dJdb):
        self.W -= self.lr*dJdW.transpose()
        self.b -= self.lr*dJdb
```
concepts.motivation_md: To train a neural network, we must calculate how changes in weights and biases affect the loss. For linear layers, these gradients allow us to update parameters and propagate error signals back to previous layers efficiently using standard matrix algebra.
concepts.recap_md: - The gradient with respect to the input is the product of the output gradient and the weight matrix.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a Pointwise Nonlinearity
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation for pointwise nonlinearities involves an element-wise multiplication of the incoming gradient by the derivative of the activation function.
concepts.content:
Pointwise nonlinearities have very simple `backward` functions. For a parameterless scalar nonlinearity $h: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with derivative $h^{\prime}$, a pointwise layer is defined as $f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) = [h(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^\mathsf{T}$. The Jacobian is a diagonal matrix of the derivatives: $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = \texttt{diag}([h^\prime(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h^\prime(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^\mathsf{T}) \triangleq \mathbf{H}^\prime$. Since there are no parameters, the backward operation only calculates $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{H}^\prime$.

(see figure: Matrix multiply for \texttt{backward} of a pointwise layer.)

This simplifies to an element-wise product:
$$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}[i] = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}[i]h^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[i]) \quad \forall i$$

(see figure: Matrix multiply for \texttt{backward} of a pointwise layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: Nonlinearities are essential for neural networks to learn complex patterns. We need a way to pass gradients through these functions so that layers earlier in the network can be updated based on the final loss.
concepts.recap_md: - The Jacobian of a pointwise nonlinearity is a diagonal matrix of its derivatives.

slots.example:
Pointwise nonlinearities have very simple `backward` functions. For a parameterless scalar nonlinearity $h: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with derivative $h^{\prime}$, a pointwise layer is defined as $f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) = [h(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^\mathsf{T}$. The Jacobian is a diagonal matrix of the derivatives: $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = \texttt{diag}([h^\prime(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h^\prime(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^\mathsf{T}) \triangleq \mathbf{H}^\prime$. Since there are no parameters, the backward operation only calculates $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{H}^\prime$.

(see figure: Matrix multiply for \texttt{backward} of a pointwise layer.)

This simplifies to an element-wise product:
$$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}[i] = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}[i]h^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[i]) \quad \forall i$$

(see figure: Matrix multiply for \texttt{backward} of a pointwise layer.)

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a ReLU Layer
concepts.one_liner: The backward pass for a ReLU layer acts as a mask, passing gradients only where the input was non-negative.
concepts.content:
For a `relu` layer, the derivative function is:
$$\begin{aligned} h^\prime(x) = \begin{cases} 1 &\text{if} \quad x \geq 0\\ 0 &\text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$
As a matrix multiply, the `backward` operation uses this derivative to gate the incoming gradients.
concepts.motivation_md: ReLU is a standard activation function. Its gradient is computationally efficient (either 0 or 1), allowing for fast backpropagation while avoiding vanishing gradients for positive inputs.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of ReLU is 1 for positive inputs and 0 for negative inputs.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for an L2 Loss Layer
concepts.one_liner: The backward signal from an $L_2$ loss layer is a row vector representing the per-dimension errors between the prediction and the target.
concepts.content:
For an $L_2$ loss function $\left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert^2_2$, where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the prediction and $\mathbf{y}$ is the ground truth, the layer has no parameters. We only derive the gradient with respect to the input:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} &= \frac{\partial \left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert^2_2}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{y}}} = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) \\ \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}*2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) \end{aligned}$$
Because the output of the loss layer is the cost $J$, $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial J} = 1$. The backward signal is a row vector of per-dimension errors.

(see figure: Matrix multiply for `backward` of an $L_2$ loss layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: The loss layer is the starting point of backpropagation. We need to calculate the initial gradient of the loss with respect to the network's final output to begin the chain rule process.
concepts.recap_md: - The gradient of the $L_2$ loss with respect to the network output is twice the difference between the prediction and the ground truth.

concepts.title: Backpropagation through an MLP
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation through an MLP involves sequential matrix multiplications where the backward pass for linear layers uses transposed weight matrices.
concepts.content:
In an MLP, the forward pass involves sequential transformations through linear and nonlinear layers.

(see figure: Forward pass through an MLP.)

For the backward pass, if we treat gradients $\mathbf{g}$ as column vectors, the operation for a linear layer becomes $\mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{W}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$. This reveals that the backward pass for a linear layer is the same operation as the forward pass, just with the weights transposed. 

(see figure: Backward pass through an MLP.)

In contrast, the `relu` layer acts as a gating matrix parameterized by the forward pass activations, masking out gradients where the activation was negative. Parameter gradients at each step are computed as an outer product between the layer's input activations $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and the gradients $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: To train multi-layer networks, we need a systematic way to apply the chain rule across many layers. Understanding the MLP backward pass as a sequence of matrix operations allows for efficient implementation in modern hardware.
concepts.recap_md: - The backward pass through linear layers uses the transpose of the forward weight matrices.

concepts.title: Backpropagation as a Neural Network
concepts.one_liner: The entire backpropagation process can be viewed as a single large neural network where the backward pass is a linear network parameterized by the forward pass.
concepts.content:
The backward pass through a neural network can be implemented as another neural network, specifically a linear network with parameters determined by the weight matrices and activations of the original network. Consequently, the full backpropagation algorithm—comprising both the forward and backward passes—can be viewed as one large neural network. Parameter gradients are computed from this network via one additional matrix multiply for each layer of the backward network.

(see figure: The computation graph for backpropagation through a three-layer MLP. It's just another neural net! Solid lines are involved in computing data/activation gradients and dotted lines are involved in...)
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing backpropagation as a neural network itself helps in understanding the symmetry between forward and backward passes and facilitates the design of automated differentiation systems.
concepts.recap_md: - Backpropagation is a composite computation graph consisting of both forward and backward passes.

concepts.title: Hypernetwork
concepts.one_liner: A hypernetwork is a neural network setup where one network outputs the values that parameterize another neural network.
concepts.content: A hypernetwork is a general setup where one neural network outputs values that parameterize another neural network. In the context of backpropagation, the forward network acts as a hypernetwork that parameterizes the backward network, such as when activations from `relu` layers are transformed to become parameters (gating masks) for the linear layers of the backward pass.
concepts.motivation_md: Hypernetworks provide a flexible framework for dynamic parameter generation, allowing a model to adapt its behavior based on the specific input it receives.
concepts.recap_md: - Hypernetworks are networks that generate parameters for other networks.

concepts.title: Linearity of the Backward Pass
concepts.one_liner: The backward pass of any computation graph consists exclusively of linear layers because the chain rule is a product of Jacobian matrices.
concepts.content: The backward network consists only of linear layers, regardless of the forward network's composition. This occurs because backpropagation implements the chain rule, which is always a product of Jacobian matrices. Since a Jacobian is a matrix, it represents a linear function. Intuitively, each Jacobian can be viewed as a locally linear approximation to the loss surface, which is represented by a linear layer in the backward pass.
concepts.motivation_md: This property explains why backpropagation is computationally predictable and why it can be implemented efficiently using standard linear algebra libraries.
concepts.recap_md: - The backward pass is always linear because it is composed of Jacobian matrix multiplications.

concepts.title: Backpropagation through DAGs

position.section_title: Backpropagation through DAGs: Branch and Merge

concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation can be extended to Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) by introducing special merge and branch modules to handle nodes with multiple inputs and outputs.
concepts.content:
Backpropagation is not limited to chain-like graphs; it can also handle Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). In a DAG, nodes can have multiple inputs and multiple outputs. To work with general DAGs, it helps to introduce two special modules that construct the topology of the graph: `merge` and `branch` (see figure: The `merge` and `branch` layers.).

Mathematically, these are defined as variable concatenation and copying:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{merge}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b) &\triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b] \triangleq \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}\\
    \texttt{branch}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) &\triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}] \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^b]
\end{aligned}$$

The shape of the data tensors (e.g., images as two-dimensional arrays) does not impact the underlying math. The `merge` operator concatenates inputs, and its backward pass simply picks out the corresponding parts of the gradient vector. The `branch` operator sends copies of the same output to multiple downstream nodes; its backward pass sums the gradients coming back from those different paths. Both modules have no parameters, so no parameter gradients are needed. These layers allow for the construction of any DAG computation graph (see figure: Merge and branch layers `forward` and `backward`.).
concepts.motivation_md: Standard backpropagation is often introduced for simple sequential chains. However, modern neural architectures like ResNets or Inception modules involve complex branching and merging. Extending backprop to DAGs allows for the training of these more sophisticated and non-linear topologies.
concepts.recap_md: - Backpropagation handles DAGs by using `merge` (concatenation) and `branch` (copying) operations.

Extending backprop to DAGs allows for the training of these more sophisticated and non-linear topologies.

concepts.title: Merge Operator

position.section_title: Backpropagation through DAGs: Branch and Merge

concepts.one_liner: The merge operator constructs graph topology by concatenating multiple input variables into a single multidimensional output.
concepts.content:
The `merge` operator is a special module used to construct the topology of Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) (see figure: The `merge` and `branch` layers.). It takes two inputs and concatenates them to result in a new multidimensional variable:
$$\texttt{merge}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b) \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b] \triangleq \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$$

While binary merging is standard, $N$-way merging can be done analogously or by repeating the operator. The backward pass equation is straightforward: to compute the gradient of the cost with respect to an input $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}$, we have:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^{a} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}^a} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}} \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}\\
    &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\Big[\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}, \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{b}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}\Big]^\mathsf{T}\\
    &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}[1, 0]^\mathsf{T}
\end{aligned}$$
This means the backward pass simply picks out the first half of the $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ gradient vector for $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^a$ and the second half for $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^b$.
concepts.motivation_md: The merge operator is necessary for layers that require multiple distinct inputs, such as combining features from different branches of a neural network into a single vector for further processing.
concepts.recap_md: - The merge operator concatenates multiple inputs into a single multidimensional variable.

concepts.title: Branch Operator

position.section_title: Backpropagation through DAGs: Branch and Merge

concepts.one_liner: The branch operator sends copies of a single input to multiple downstream nodes, resulting in the summation of gradients during the backward pass.
concepts.content:
The `branch` operator is a module used to construct Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) by sending copies of the same output to multiple downstream nodes (see figure: The `merge` and `branch` layers.). Mathematically, it is defined as:
$$\texttt{branch}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}] \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^b]$$

In the backward pass, the module receives multiple gradients from different downstream paths, represented as the gradient vector $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} = [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b]$. The backward pass output is computed as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}&= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}\\
    &= [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b] \frac{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^b]}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}}\\
    &= [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b] [1, 1]^\mathsf{T}\\
    &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a + \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b
\end{aligned}$$
Thus, branching simply sums all the gradients passed backward to it. While binary branching is shown, $N$-way branching follows the same logic.
concepts.motivation_md: Branching allows a single piece of data or a parameter to influence multiple parts of a model. Summing the gradients during backpropagation ensures that the total influence of that variable on the final loss is correctly accounted for.
concepts.recap_md: - The branch operator copies a single input to multiple outputs.

concepts.title: Parameter Sharing
concepts.one_liner: Parameter sharing occurs when a single parameter is sent as input to multiple layers, causing their gradients to sum during backpropagation.
concepts.content:
Parameter sharing consists of a single parameter being sent as input to multiple different layers. This can be viewed as a branching operation in the computation graph (see figure: Parameter sharing is equivalent to branching a parameter in the computation graph.). Because it functions as a branch, gradients summate for shared parameters. If $\{\theta^i\}^N_{i=1}$ is a set of variables that are all copies of one free parameter $\theta$, then:
$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta} = \sum_i \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta^i}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Parameter sharing reduces the number of free parameters in a model, which can prevent overfitting and allow the model to learn features that are invariant across different parts of the input (like in convolutional layers).
concepts.recap_md: - Parameter sharing is equivalent to a branching operation in a computation graph.

concepts.title: Backpropagation to the Data
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation treats data and parameters symmetrically, allowing the optimization of input data to minimize a loss function.
concepts.content:
Backpropagation does not distinguish between parameters and data; it treats both as generic inputs to parameterless modules. Consequently, backprop can be used to optimize data inputs to the graph just like parameter inputs. In the forward direction, the inputs are data and parameters, and the output is the loss. In the backward direction, the output includes gradients of the loss with respect to both the data and parameters (see figure: Full forward and backward passes for a learning problem $\min J(\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{y},\theta)$, collapsed into a single computation block.).

In frameworks like PyTorch, input variables are the 'leaves' of the computation graph and can be set as optimization targets. This symmetry allows for applications such as visualizing the input image that most activates a specific neuron. By defining the loss $J$ as the negative value of a target neuron's activation, one can use backprop to find an image that maximizes that activation (see figure: Visualizing the optimal image of a cat according to a particular neural net.). This is a useful method for identifying the visual features a neuron is sensitive to.
concepts.motivation_md: Optimizing input data allows researchers to 'see' what a neural network has learned. By finding the input that maximizes a specific neuron's response, we can interpret the internal representations of complex black-box models.
concepts.recap_md: - Backpropagation can calculate gradients for input data as well as model parameters.

Batch mode backpropagation is a method for performing the backward pass across an entire set of inputs simultaneously.
To compute gradients in batch mode, one must first perform a forward pass for all datapoints in the batch.

overlay.rationale: The generic backward function is a concrete implementation of the abstract backward operation concept.
The ReLU backward pass is a specific, simplified instance of backpropagation for a pointwise nonlinearity where the derivative is a binary mask.
Viewing backpropagation as a network illustrates how intermediate values (like activations) are reused to parameterize the backward pass.
The relationship between the forward and backward passes in backpropagation is a primary example of a hypernetwork setup.
The rule that gradients of shared parameters sum together is a direct application of the linearity of the gradient operator.
Backpropagation through DAGs generalizes the chain-like backpropagation used in standard Multilayer Perceptrons.
Merge and branch are the two complementary operators used to define the topology of general DAGs.
The backward operation is described as the modular counterpart to the forward pass, performing the reverse operation in the computation graph.
This theorem provides the rigorous mathematical justification for the gradient summation and averaging used in batch-mode backpropagation.
